text.title: LS / Gumroad Pricing Flip Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules for a LemonSqueezy/Gumroad price flip: explicit grandfathering, net-of-fee-and-VAT comparison rather than sticker price, cohort tagging by variant instead of timestamp, the refund-window trap on a price cut, an enumerated list of every surface that hardcodes the old price, an honest confound statement for sequential cohorts, and the preconditions that make the flip unreadable.

rule.statement: The record MUST state, as one of `grandfather` / `migrate-all` / `migrate-on-renewal`, what happens to existing subscribers — and if not `grandfather`, name the concrete mechanism: the LemonSqueezy `PATCH /v1/subscriptions/{id}` call with the new `variant_id` (recording the `invoice_immediately` and proration settings used), or the Gumroad membership price-change flow with its member notification. The count of subscriptions to be touched MUST be recorded before the flip.

rationale.source: LemonSqueezy API — update subscription (variant_id, invoice_immediately, disable_prorations); Gumroad membership pricing

rule.rationale: Editing a variant's price on either platform changes the price for new checkouts only; existing subscriptions keep billing at the amount they were created with. So the default outcome of "we raised the price" is a permanently split book where MRR-per-customer never moves — and the operator reading a flat MRR curve two months later concludes the price rise failed, when it simply never reached anyone.

rule.statement: Before/after comparison MUST use net payout per sale, not the list price. The record MUST capture the platform fee schedule in force at flip time (LemonSqueezy: percentage plus fixed per-transaction fee; Gumroad: flat per-sale percentage) and whether the store is configured tax-inclusive or tax-exclusive, with the buyer-country mix of the compared cohorts.

rationale.source: Merchant-of-record model — LemonSqueezy and Gumroad published fee schedules; EU VAT (destination-based rates)

rule.rationale: Both platforms are merchants of record, so VAT is settled per buyer country. Under tax-inclusive pricing the sticker price is fixed and your net moves with the buyer's rate — the same €50 nets materially less from a 23% country than from a 0% one — which means a cohort whose geography shifted can show a net-revenue change with no pricing effect at all. The fixed per-transaction component compounds this at low price points, where it is a far larger share of a $9 sale than of a $99 one.

rule.statement: Cohort assignment MUST be derived from the order's variant/product identifier — LemonSqueezy `variant_id` from the `order_created` / `subscription_created` webhook payload, or the Gumroad product permalink plus offer code — and stored on the order record. Splitting cohorts by `created_at` relative to the flip timestamp is rejected.

rationale.source: LemonSqueezy webhook payloads (order_created, subscription_created); Gumroad offer-code URL form /l/{permalink}/{code}

rule.rationale: A timestamp split misclassifies every order whose checkout was opened before the flip and completed after it, plus retried and delayed payments, and it silently breaks when dashboard timestamps are read in a different timezone from the analytics store. The variant id is what the buyer actually paid against, so it stays correct under all three.

rule.statement: For any price decrease the record MUST state the store's active refund window and the goodwill policy for buyers inside it (refund-and-rebuy allowed / partial credit / nothing), plus the count of orders currently within that window and the worst-case refund exposure in currency.
rule.rationale: A buyer who paid full price yesterday and sees a 40% cut today has a mechanical arbitrage: request the refund the window entitles them to, then repurchase at the new price. The loss is not only the delta but the platform fee on both transactions, and an elevated refund rate in the same window is what payment processors read as a dispute-risk signal — so the cut looks self-funding until the refund queue arrives.

rule.statement: The record MUST enumerate every surface carrying the old price and its owner: hosted checkout links and overlay/embed buy buttons, discount and offer codes with their fixed amounts, affiliate links, the pricing page and any CDN-cached copy of it with its TTL, README and docs, lifecycle emails, and app-store or third-party listing copy. Each entry is marked updated or deliberately left, before the flip is declared complete.
rule.rationale: A fixed-amount discount code written against the old price becomes a different percentage after the flip and can invert to below cost on a cut; a cached pricing page keeps advertising the old figure for the full TTL while checkout charges the new one, which is the single most common source of "the site said $29" support tickets and chargeback disputes after a rise.

rule.statement: Because neither platform splits live traffic across price points natively, the record MUST label the design `sequential` and list the confounds present in the comparison window: traffic-source mix, launch or campaign spikes, seasonality, and any concurrent landing-page change. Subscription verdicts MUST NOT be read before one full billing cycle has elapsed past the flip. A flip run concurrently with any other pricing-page change is recorded as `not-attributable`.

rationale.source: Internal — sequential-cohort inference on merchant-of-record platforms

rule.rationale: A time-based split makes the flip perfectly collinear with everything else that changed on that date, so a Product Hunt spike or a seasonal trough is indistinguishable from price elasticity. Subscriptions add a lag confound: churn and involuntary-failure effects of a price change only appear at the next renewal, so a conversion-rate win read at week two routinely reverses once the first billing cycle completes.

rule.statement: Skip when ANY holds: (a) fewer than roughly 30 paid conversions in the comparison window — the difference will sit inside noise whatever the arithmetic says, (b) pricing is contractually fixed (enterprise, regulated, existing annual commitments), (c) another pricing-page or funnel change is shipping in the same window, making attribution impossible, (d) the store has no webhook or export capturing variant id per order, so cohorts cannot be reconstructed after the fact.
rule.rationale: Each rule above depends on being able to attribute a revenue difference to the price. Without volume, without exclusivity of the change, or without per-order variant data, the flip may still be a fine business decision — but the decision record would document a measurement that cannot be made, which is worse than recording it as a judgement call.
